libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: The impedance equation
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: The whole lab in one equation: $\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{e} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{u})$ with $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{R}^\top(\mathbf{x}_d - \mathbf{x})$ and $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{v}$. Spring, line guide, plane guide and damping field differ only in the diagonals of $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. A zero on the diagonal of $\mathbf{K}$ means 'free along that axis'.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: The wall equation
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: The wall is the plane through $\mathbf{x}_d$ with outward normal $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{R}(0,0,1)^\top$. The depth $d = \mathbf{n}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_d - \mathbf{x})$ is positive inside the wall. The force $\max(0, k_z d - b_z\,\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{n}$ can push you out but never pull you in.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: Roll, pitch, yaw to a rotation matrix
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: Builds $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}_z(\psi)\mathbf{R}_y(\theta)\mathbf{R}_x(\phi)$ from roll $\phi$ = `rpy.x()`, pitch $\theta$ = `rpy.y()` and yaw $\psi$ = `rpy.z()`, all in radians. Each `AngleAxisd` is one elementary rotation and `*` chains them in the same order as the maths. Example: yaw = 90 degrees turns $(1,0,0)$ into $(0,1,0)$.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: What a scenario holds
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: Everything the force needs: which kind, the target pose $(\mathbf{x}_d, \mathbf{R})$ stored as a point and three angles, the stiffness $(k_x, k_y, k_z)$ in N/m, the damping $(b_x, b_y, b_z)$ in N s/m, and three compiled custom equations. Stiffness and damping are measured along the axes of the target frame, not the device frame.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: THE function
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: The engine calls this every millisecond with the newest position $\mathbf{x}$ (m), velocity $\mathbf{v}$ (m/s) and time $t$ (s), and sends the result in newtons. There is no safety code in here on purpose: the engine fades the force in, caps it and switches it off, for every scenario alike.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: Look from the target frame
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: First the orientation $\mathbf{R}$, then the position error $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{R}^\top(\mathbf{x}_d - \mathbf{x})$ and the velocity $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{v}$, both seen from the target frame. $\mathbf{R}^\top$ is used instead of $\mathbf{R}^{-1}$ because, for a rotation, they are equal. The error points from the cursor towards the target.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.match: const Vec3 f_local = s.k.asDiagonal() * e - s.b.asDiagonal() * u;
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: Spring minus damper
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: This line is $\mathbf{f}_{\text{local}} = \mathbf{K}\mathbf{e} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{u}$. `asDiagonal()` turns the vector $(k_x, k_y, k_z)$ into $\operatorname{diag}(k_x, k_y, k_z)$. Example: $k = 300$ N/m and 1 cm of error give 3 N.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: Back to the device frame
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: The force was worked out in the target frame; $\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{f}_{\text{local}}$ writes it in the device frame, which is what the motors understand. Only $\mathbf{R}$ is used, no translation, because a force is a direction.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: Penetration depth
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: The third component of $\mathbf{e}$ is $d = \mathbf{n}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_d - \mathbf{x})$, how deep you are inside the wall (m). Outside ($d \le 0$) the wall does nothing at all.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.match: const double push = std::max(0.0, s.k.z() * d - s.b.z() * u.z());
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: Push, never pull
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: $\max(0, k_z d - b_z\,\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{v})$. Example: $k = 500$ N/m, $b = 3$ N s/m, 4 mm inside: moving in at 0.1 m/s gives 2.3 N; pulling out at 1 m/s would give $-1$ N, a pull into the wall, so `max` makes it 0.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: The wall normal
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: The outward normal $\mathbf{n}$ is the third column of $\mathbf{R}$, the rotated z axis. With rpy = 0 it is the device $+z$ axis; with pitch = 90 degrees it is $+x$. The force is the push times $\mathbf{n}$.

libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.title: Your equations, every 1 ms
libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h.text: For the custom scenario the variables are copied into an array in the order of `my::Expr::Var` (x y z vx vy vz t xd yd zd kx ky kz bx by bz), and the three compiled equations are evaluated. Custom equations are in the device frame: rpy is not applied here.

libs/myEXPR.h.title: What you may type
libs/myEXPR.h.text: Numbers, `+ - * / ^`, parentheses, the variables, `pi`, and the listed functions. There is no `if` or `<`: use `step(a)`, which is 1 when $a > 0$ and 0 otherwise. Example: `max(0, kz*(zd - z) - bz*vz)*step(zd - z)` is a wall.

libs/myEXPR.h.match: enum Var { X, Y, Z, VX
libs/myEXPR.h.title: The variables and their order
libs/myEXPR.h.text: These 16 names are all you can use, and they are case sensitive (`X` is an error). Their order is the layout of the `vars[]` array that the scenario code fills every millisecond, so the two lists must stay in step.

libs/myEXPR.h.match: bool compile(const std::string& text, std::string& err) {
libs/myEXPR.h.title: Compile once
libs/myEXPR.h.text: Turns your text into a short stack program, once, when you press send. On a mistake it returns false with a message such as `unknown name 'X' at position 1`, and keeps the previous program. Parsing text is slow; doing it once keeps the 1 kHz loop fast.

libs/myEXPR.h.title: Stack depth check
libs/myEXPR.h.text: Counts how deep the stack can get and refuses equations that need more than 32 slots. This guarantees that `eval()` never writes past the end of its fixed array, a classic C++ bug.

libs/myEXPR.h.title: Evaluate every 1 ms
libs/myEXPR.h.text: Runs the stack program: numbers and variables are pushed, operators pop their inputs and push the result. No memory is allocated, so it takes well under a microsecond. A division by zero gives an infinite value, which the engine replaces by zero force.

libs/myEXPR.h.title: step(a)
libs/myEXPR.h.text: $\operatorname{step}(a) = 1$ if $a > 0$, else 0. Multiply a force by `step(zd - z)` and it only acts when $z < z_d$, which is how you build one-sided forces like walls.

libs/myEXPR.h.match: static double clamp3(double v, double lo, double hi)
libs/myEXPR.h.title: clamp(value, lo, hi)
libs/myEXPR.h.text: Keeps a value inside $[\text{lo}, \text{hi}]$. Use it to cap a force that could grow too large, for example a magnet: `clamp(..., -1.5, 1.5)` never asks for more than 1.5 N on that axis.

libs/myEXPR.h.title: Recursive descent: + and -
libs/myEXPR.h.text: The parser has one function per precedence level: `expr` handles `+ -`, `term` handles `* /`, `unary` a leading minus, `power` the `^`. Each one calls the next, tighter level, so `1 + 2*3` is read as $1 + (2 \cdot 3)$.

libs/myEXPR.h.title: Powers bind tightest
libs/myEXPR.h.text: `^` is right-associative: `2^3^2` is $2^{(3^2)} = 512$. Because the exponent is parsed as `unary`, and `unary` sits above `power`, `-x^2` means $-(x^2)$, as in maths.

libs/myEXPR.h.title: Names become variables
libs/myEXPR.h.text: A name that is not a function and not `pi` must be one of the 16 variables. Anything else gives `unknown name '...'` with its position, so a typo can never silently become zero.

libs/myEXPR.h.match: bool call(const std::string& name, size_t start) {
libs/myEXPR.h.title: Function calls
libs/myEXPR.h.text: Looks the name up in the one-, two- and three-argument lists, then reads exactly that many arguments separated by commas. Wrong counts give messages like `'clamp' needs 3 arguments`.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: The serial protocol
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: Four kinds of message. The one used every millisecond is `0x2A` plus three floats of force (13 bytes out), answered by `0x2B` plus position and velocity (25 bytes back). `0x0A` wakes the device up; `0x1A` sends joint torques and reads joint angles. Status events `0xBA` can arrive at any time and are skipped.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: Feedback: X and V
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: After every exchange, `X` holds the cursor position $\mathbf{x}$ in metres and `V` the velocity $\mathbf{v}$ in m/s, both in the device frame. These are the numbers the lab page shows.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: Device-level force cap
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: `render_F_cmd()` scales any force with $\lVert\mathbf{F}\rVert$ above `F_max` back to 3 N. It is a second cap underneath the engine's `fmax`, so on the real device 3 N is the ceiling unless someone raises this deliberately.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.match: // Until the device is calibrated, firmware 7.x
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: Calibrated or not
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: After power-up the device has no cursor position yet: it reports $\mathbf{x} = 0$ and $\mathbf{v} = 65535$. The flag starts false and is updated after every exchange. The lab engine refuses forces while it is false.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: One round trip
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: Sends a force in newtons and reads back position and velocity, timing the round trip (about 0.15 ms). On a failure it counts the error and resynchronises the serial stream. Every read and every force in the lab goes through this function.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: The calibration test
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: If all three velocities are near 65535, the device is not calibrated. Fix: rest the cursor on the magnetic dock until the front LED changes from purple, then lift it off.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: Cap, send, reset
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: Computes $n = \lVert\mathbf{F}_{\text{cmd}}\rVert$; if $n > F_{\max}$ the whole vector is scaled by $F_{\max}/n$, which keeps its direction. A non-finite force becomes zero. The command is then reset to zero, so a force is never sent twice by accident.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: How to calibrate
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: Purple front LED = not calibrated. Rest the cursor on the magnetic dock until the LED changes colour, then lift it off. Needed after every power-up; motor power is not needed for it.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: quick_start()
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: Finds and opens the serial port, wakes the device up, reads the raw joint angles (which work even before calibration), prints the device info and 10 position samples. Every program calls this first.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: Always leave zero force
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: Sets the command to zero, sends it once, and closes the port. The destructor calls it too, so the device is never left pushing when a program ends.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: Wake-up: 0x0A
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: Sends the single byte `0x0A` up to 3 times and expects `0x0B` followed by 21 bytes: a 16-bit device id, 3 info bytes and a 16-byte UUID, which is printed as text.

libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.title: Skipping status events
libs/myHAPLY_v1.h.text: Reads one header byte. If it is the expected reply, it reads the payload; if it is a status event (`0xBA`), it reads and skips it and tries again, at most 16 times. This is what keeps the loop running smoothly on firmware 7.x.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: All the safety limits
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: $k \le 1000$ N/m, $b \le 15$ N s/m, `fmax` $\le 4$ N, speed guard 1.5 m/s. The target may move at most 0.1 m/s, $k$ may change at most 2000 N/m per second, the fade-in lasts 1 s, and the heartbeat must be younger than 1 s.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: Parameters move smoothly
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: What you ask for is a target; what is applied moves towards it a small step each millisecond. Example: moving $\mathbf{x}_d$ by 5 cm takes 0.5 s, and $k$ from 0 to 800 N/m takes 0.4 s. Dragging a slider never produces a jump in force.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.match: const Vec3 F_eq = haptics::force(scn_, x_, v_, t, &det);
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: The equation, every 1 ms
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: Calls the scenario equation of `libs/myHAPLY_SCENARIOS.h` with the newest $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $t$. `det.e` returns the error in the target frame, which is recorded in columns e1, e2, e3.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: No calibration, no forces
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: If the device loses calibration while forces are on, they switch off and the page shows `forces off: the device is not calibrated`. Dock the cursor to calibrate again.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: Heartbeat watchdog
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: While the driving page is alive, the server sends `hb` five times a second. If none arrives for 1 s, forces switch off: `forces off: the page stopped answering (watchdog)`. A closed tab or a sleeping laptop can never leave the device pushing.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: Speed guard
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: If $\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert > 1.5$ m/s, forces switch off. An unstable spring usually shows up as speed first, so this catches buzzing before it grows. The message suggests the fix: lower $k$ or raise $b$.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: Fade-in over 1 s
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: $\mathbf{F} = r\,\mathbf{F}_{\text{eq}}$ with $r$ growing by 0.001 per millisecond, from 0 to 1 in 1 s. It restarts from 0 when forces switch on or the scenario changes, so you never get a kick.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: Finite check and force cap
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: A force that is not a finite number (for example a custom equation dividing by zero) becomes zero. Then if $\lVert\mathbf{F}\rVert > f_{\max}$ the whole vector is scaled down, keeping its direction.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: Switching forces on
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: Forces can only be switched on with a calibrated device and a fresh heartbeat; otherwise the page explains why. Switching on resets the fade-in ramp to 0.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: The 1 kHz clock
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: Each cycle the next deadline moves 1 ms forward and the loop sleeps until then. If it ever falls more than 5 periods behind, it resets the clock instead of rushing to catch up.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: Recording at 1 kHz
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: While recording, every cycle appends one row (time, x, v, force sent, error in the target frame, ramp, round-trip time) to memory that was reserved in advance, so the loop never waits for the disk. Recordings stop by themselves after 600 s.

lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.title: The CSV columns
lab/engine/haply_lab_engine.cpp.text: Positions in m, velocities in m/s, forces f1..f3 in N, errors e1..e3 ($\mathbf{x}_d - \mathbf{x}$ in the target frame) in m, ramp from 0 to 1, and loop_us, the device round trip in microseconds. The file is written in a low-priority thread after you stop recording.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: Timing and quitting
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: On Windows the default sleep resolution is too coarse for 1 kHz; this object asks for 1 ms resolution while the program runs. `QuitKey` lets you press Q (or Ctrl+C) to leave the loop cleanly.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: Create and start the device
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: An empty port means 'find it automatically'. `quick_start()` opens the port, wakes the device up and prints 10 samples; if it fails, the program stops before the loop.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: Preallocated logger
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: Reserves memory for 120 s at the loop rate before the loop starts, so logging never slows the loop down.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: The loop
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: Runs until you press Q: exchange with the device, log, print now and then, sleep until the next millisecond.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: Reading = sending zero force
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: Every exchange sends a force and receives position and velocity. Here `F_cmd` is always zero, so this is a pure read and the device never pushes on your hand.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: One log row per cycle
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: Time stamps, position $\mathbf{x}$ (m), velocity $\mathbf{v}$ (m/s), the force actually sent (N) and the round-trip time. These become one line of the CSV in `logs/`.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: Device stopped answering
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: 100 failed exchanges in a row (about 0.1 s at 1 kHz, or longer with timeouts) means the cable is out or the device is off, so the program stops instead of spinning.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: Print 20 times a second
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: Printing every cycle would slow the loop down, so the status line is refreshed only at `--print-hz` (20 Hz by default). It also shows the achieved loop rate and NOT CALIBRATED when the device needs the dock.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: Keep the 1 kHz schedule
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: The next deadline moves 1 ms forward each cycle and the loop sleeps until then. If a cycle runs late it is counted, and the schedule restarts from now instead of catching up in a burst.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: Timing summary
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: At the end the program prints the mean, median, 99th percentile and maximum round-trip time. On the lab Raspberry Pi the mean is about 150 microseconds, well inside the 1 ms budget.

100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.title: Clean up
100-Haply-basics/01_read_fbk.cpp.text: Sends zero force, closes the port, then writes the CSV log to `logs/haply_log_file__Inverse3_<date>.csv`.
